subsystems.name: Accelerating structures
subsystems.role: add energy to the beam at stations spaced along the ring.

subsystems.name: Beam optics and alignment
subsystems.role: keeps a beam only micrometres wide on a track millions of kilometres long.

subsystems.name: Beam transport and vacuum
subsystems.role: either a continuous evacuated pipe or free-space drift between stations.
parts: optical relay telescopes for free-space segments

subsystems.name: Power and thermal control
subsystems.role: supplies terawatt-scale electricity and rejects the waste heat.

subsystems.name: Injector and interaction region
subsystems.role: fills the ring and focuses the two beams into collision.

subsystems.name: Beam dumps and safety
subsystems.role: absorbs the beam and guarantees no stray path can reach anything inhabited.

buildSteps.title: Fix the gradient on Earth
buildSteps.detail: Before anything flies, plasma-wakefield and superconducting modules must show they can add energy per metre reliably for long pulses, not just in short laboratory bursts.

buildSteps.title: Test beam transport at increasing range
buildSteps.detail: A ground-based vacuum or free-space line, then a longer one, measures how far a focused beam can travel before it drifts or spreads beyond tolerance.

buildSteps.title: Build robotic assembly and servicing
buildSteps.detail: Very large structures in orbit can only be made by machines, so autonomous assembly, welding, cable routing and repair must be proven on smaller platforms first.

buildSteps.title: Deploy a pilot arc
buildSteps.detail: A short arc — a few tens of kilometres, far from a full orbit — with a handful of accelerating stations, its own solar arrays and a return path, tests alignment under sunlight, thermal cycling and gravity-gradient drift.

buildSteps.title: Mass-produce the ring
buildSteps.detail: Accelerator modules, magnets, pumps and radiators are made in numbers never attempted, since a full ring needs orders of magnitude more units than any existing machine.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop and inject
buildSteps.detail: The arc is extended until the two ends meet, the vacuum or optical path becomes continuous, and a low-energy beam is circulated for the first time.

buildSteps.title: Ramp and collide
buildSteps.detail: Energy is raised step by step while the alignment system holds the orbit, then the two beams are focused into collision in the interaction region.

buildSteps.title: Operate and repair
buildSteps.detail: Detectors record events, heat is radiated away, and robotic servicing replaces failed stations without shutting down the whole ring.

prerequisites.why: gigavolt-per-metre gradients have been demonstrated in plasma over centimetres; a ring needs them sustained over metres and repeated thousands of times.

prerequisites.tech: Superconducting magnets and RF at industrial scale
prerequisites.why: the technology works, but the quantity required is beyond any current supply chain.
robotic arms and servicing missions exist; nothing has assembled and aligned a structure hundreds of thousands of kilometres long.
spacecraft solar arrays currently deliver kilowatts to megawatts, so collector area and heat rejection must grow by many orders of magnitude.
laser ranging and interplanetary laser links work over millions of kilometres, but not to the sub-micrometre beam tolerances an accelerator needs.

prerequisites.tech: Overcoming synchrotron radiation in a ring
prerequisites.why: in a circular machine the energy lost per turn rises with the fourth power of beam energy and falls only linearly with radius, so beyond some energy even a solar-orbit ring radiates more than it can replace — the geometry itself becomes the ceiling.

pathway.milestone: Earth-based high-gradient acceleration experiments and feasibility studies for roughly 100 km circular colliders
pathway.unlocks: realistic figures for achievable gradient, cost per GeV and magnet production.

pathway.milestone: Free-space and evacuated beam-transport tests over hundreds of kilometres, plus robotic assembly trials of large space structures
pathway.unlocks: confidence that a beam can be held on a very long baseline and that the structure can be built and serviced.

pathway.milestone: A pilot arc: tens of kilometres of accelerator in orbit, solar powered, with a returning beam path and beam dump
pathway.unlocks: continuous operation, alignment control and repair practice at unprecedented scale.

pathway.milestone: A closed ring around a planetary orbit with injector, interaction region and detectors
pathway.unlocks: collision energies limited by circumference rather than by the size of any site — while the synchrotron-radiation ceiling is finally tested in practice.

pathway.milestone: Linear geometry or beams steered by stellar plasma and magnetic structures
pathway.unlocks: the only known route past the ring's radiation limit — a machine whose scale is set by astrophysics, not engineering.
